---
title: "Compound Compositions in ZPF Data"
---

[Phase diagram (ZPF) data](dataset_schema.qmd#phase_boundary_data) give the composition of each phase in a phase region.
ESPEI uses the known phase compositions in two ways [@bocklund2019]:

1. The *target hyperplane* is the average of the chemical potentials of the equilibria at each known phase composition.
2. The *driving force* of each phase is the distance of its Gibbs energy at its phase composition below the target hyperplane.

Both need phases that can vary their composition in every direction of the composition space of the dataset.
Stoichiometric compounds, e.g. `(A)1(B)2`, can't vary their composition at all.
Other phases can vary their composition in some directions only: `(A,B)2(C)1` in an A-B-C system can change the ratio of A to B, but always has X(C) = 1/3, and a binary phase in a ternary dataset has none of the third component.

**ESPEI uses known compositions of these phases as unknown (`null`).**
Datasets should keep the measured phase compositions; there's no need to change them.

## Their chemical potentials are not determined

The chemical potentials of an equilibrium are the values of the plane tangent to the Gibbs energies of its phases at the pure components.
A phase that can vary its composition has one tangent at each composition.
A stoichiometric compound has a Gibbs energy at one composition only, and every line through that point is tangent to it.

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| fig-cap: "Gibbs energies of a solution phase, (A,B), and a stoichiometric compound, AB~2~. The tangent to the solution phase is unique, so are its chemical potentials, the values of the tangent at X(B) = 0 and 1. Any line through the compound is tangent to it."
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

RT = 8.314 * 1000  # J/mol at 1000 K

def xlogx(x):
    return x * np.log(x)

def G_solution(x):
    return -4000 * x + RT * (xlogx(x) + xlogx(1 - x)) - 20000 * x * (1 - x)

def slope(G, x, dx=1e-6):
    return (G(x + dx) - G(x - dx)) / (2 * dx)

fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 3.6), sharey=True, layout="constrained")
x = np.linspace(1e-4, 1 - 1e-4, 400)
x0 = 0.35
mu = G_solution(x0) + slope(G_solution, x0) * (np.array([0, 1]) - x0)  # chemical potentials of A and B
axs[0].plot(x, G_solution(x), color="C0", lw=2, label="(A,B)")
axs[0].plot([0, 1], mu, "o-", color="k", lw=1, ms=5, clip_on=False)
axs[0].plot(x0, G_solution(x0), "o", color="C0", ms=8, mec="k")
axs[0].annotate("$\\mu_A$", (0, mu[0]), xytext=(6, 4), textcoords="offset points")
axs[0].annotate("$\\mu_B$", (1, mu[1]), xytext=(-18, 4), textcoords="offset points")
axs[0].set_title("(A,B): one tangent")

x_AB2, G_AB2 = 2 / 3, -9000
for s in np.linspace(-14000, 8000, 7):
    axs[1].plot([0, 1], G_AB2 + s * (np.array([0, 1]) - x_AB2), "o-", color="0.5", lw=1, ms=4, clip_on=False)
axs[1].plot(x_AB2, G_AB2, "o", color="C1", ms=8, mec="k", label="AB$_2$")
axs[1].set_title("AB$_2$: every line through it")
for ax in axs:
    ax.set(xlim=(0, 1), xlabel="X(B)")
    ax.legend(loc="lower left")
axs[0].set_ylabel("G (J/mol)")
plt.show()
```

In equilibrium with other phases, the other phases determine which tangent is the one for the equilibrium, e.g. the common tangent of the compound and a liquid.
The chemical potentials of an equilibrium at the composition of the compound alone are not determined; PyCalphad returns one set of them, which need not be the one of the equilibrium in the data, so they can't be used for the target hyperplane.

A phase that can vary its composition in some directions only is tangent to many planes, too.
The Gibbs energy of `(A,B)2(C)1` is a curve in a G-X(A)-X(B) plot, and every plane containing a tangent line of the curve is tangent to it.

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| fig-cap: "Gibbs energies of a ternary solution phase, (A,B,C), and an (A,B)~2~(C)~1~ phase, which has X(C) = 1/3 (dashed line). The tangent plane of the solution phase is unique, so are its chemical potentials, the values of the plane at the pure components (dots on the vertical lines). Tangent planes of (A,B)~2~(C)~1~ rotate about the tangent line of its Gibbs energy curve."
def G_ternary(xa, xb):
    xc = 1 - xa - xb
    return -3000 * xa - 1000 * xb + RT * (xlogx(xa) + xlogx(xb) + xlogx(xc)) - 15000 * (xa * xb + xa * xc + xb * xc)

def G_A2C_B2C(y):
    """Gibbs energy per mole of atoms with the site fraction y of A, at X(A) = 2y/3, X(B) = 2(1-y)/3 and X(C) = 1/3"""
    return -14000 * y - 11000 * (1 - y) + 2 / 3 * (RT * (xlogx(y) + xlogx(1 - y)) - 8000 * y * (1 - y))

corners = np.array([[1, 0], [0, 1], [0, 0]])  # X(A) and X(B) of pure A, B and C
zmin, zmax = -32, 2  # kJ/mol

def draw_plane(ax, mu, color, alpha):
    ax.plot_trisurf(corners[:, 0], corners[:, 1], mu / 1000, color=color, alpha=alpha, edgecolor="none", shade=False)
    ax.scatter(corners[:, 0], corners[:, 1], mu / 1000, color=color, s=14, depthshade=False)

def draw_axes(ax, title):
    for (xa, xb), name in zip(corners, "ABC"):
        ax.plot([xa, xa], [xb, xb], [zmin, zmax], color="0.3", lw=0.8)
        ax.text(xa, xb, zmax + 1, name, ha="center")
    ax.plot([1, 0, 0, 1], [0, 1, 0, 0], [zmin] * 4, color="0.3", lw=0.8)
    ax.set(xlabel="X(A)", ylabel="X(B)", zlabel="G (kJ/mol)", zlim=(zmin, zmax), title=title)
    ax.view_init(elev=15, azim=-55)
    ax.set_box_aspect(None, zoom=0.9)

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(10, 4), layout="constrained")
ax = fig.add_subplot(1, 2, 1, projection="3d")
xa, xb = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(1e-3, 1, 60), np.linspace(1e-3, 1, 60))
xa, xb = xa[xa + xb < 1 - 1e-3], xb[xa + xb < 1 - 1e-3]
ax.plot_trisurf(xa, xb, G_ternary(xa, xb) / 1000, color="C0", alpha=0.35, edgecolor="none")
xa0, xb0 = 0.3, 0.35
dGa = slope(lambda xa: G_ternary(xa, xb0), xa0)
dGb = slope(lambda xb: G_ternary(xa0, xb), xb0)
mu_C = G_ternary(xa0, xb0) - xa0 * dGa - xb0 * dGb
draw_plane(ax, np.array([mu_C + dGa, mu_C + dGb, mu_C]), "k", 0.3)
ax.scatter(xa0, xb0, G_ternary(xa0, xb0) / 1000, color="C0", s=40, edgecolor="k", depthshade=False)
ax.plot([xa0, xa0], [xb0, xb0], [zmin, G_ternary(xa0, xb0) / 1000], color="C0", ls=":")
draw_axes(ax, "(A,B,C): one tangent plane")

ax = fig.add_subplot(1, 2, 2, projection="3d")
y = np.linspace(1e-3, 1 - 1e-3, 200)
ax.plot(2 * y / 3, 2 * (1 - y) / 3, G_A2C_B2C(y) / 1000, color="C1", lw=3)
ax.plot([2 / 3, 0], [0, 2 / 3], [zmin, zmin], color="C1", ls="--", lw=1)
y0 = 0.4
X0 = np.array([2 * y0 / 3, 2 * (1 - y0) / 3, 1 / 3])
# Tangent planes have MU(A) - MU(B) = 3/2 dG/dy and pass through G at X0. Adding t*(1, 1, -2) to MU rotates the plane about the tangent line.
mu = np.array([1.5 * slope(G_A2C_B2C, y0), 0, 0])
mu += G_A2C_B2C(y0) - mu @ X0
for t, color in zip([-5000, 0, 5000], ["C2", "C3", "C4"]):
    draw_plane(ax, mu + t * np.array([1, 1, -2]), color, 0.25)
ax.scatter(X0[0], X0[1], G_A2C_B2C(y0) / 1000, color="C1", s=40, edgecolor="k", depthshade=False)
ax.plot([X0[0], X0[0]], [X0[1], X0[1]], [zmin, G_A2C_B2C(y0) / 1000], color="C1", ls=":")
draw_axes(ax, "(A,B)$_2$(C)$_1$: planes rotate about a line")
plt.show()
```

## Driving forces at unknown compositions

A measured composition is generally not one that these phases can take, e.g. AB~2~ measured at X(B) = 0.667 rather than 2/3, or `(A,B)2(C)1` measured at X(C) = 0.34.
The phase has no Gibbs energy there.
As for any unknown phase composition, ESPEI uses the largest driving force of any composition of the phase:

- A stoichiometric compound has one composition, so its driving force is exact.
- For a phase that can vary its composition in some directions only, the driving force is not the one at the measured composition, so where the measured composition is along the phase's range of compositions isn't fit. ESPEI warns when it uses known compositions of these phases as unknown.

## Phase regions without a target hyperplane

A phase region needs a known composition of a phase that can vary its composition in every direction to define the target hyperplane.
Without one, e.g. `[["AB2", ["B"], [0.667]], ["LIQUID", ["B"], [null]]]` or a phase region of two compounds, the driving forces of the phase region are zero and ESPEI warns about it.

To use these phase regions, give compositions of the target hyperplane as phase compositions of `__HYPERPLANE__`.
The target hyperplane is then the average of the chemical potentials of the equilibria at the `__HYPERPLANE__` compositions, instead of at the phase compositions.
Choose a composition where the phases of the region are in equilibrium, e.g. the overall composition of an alloy, or, as here, a composition between the compound and the liquid:

```json
[["__HYPERPLANE__", ["B"], [0.7]], ["AB2", ["B"], [0.667]], ["LIQUID", ["B"], [null]]]
```

ESPEI still computes the driving force of each phase of the region to this target hyperplane.
